picoos: PicoOS borrows Unix interface names and conventions, but implements a small subset and does not claim POSIX conformance.
113-system-v-abi-stack-frames-and-call-c: The ABI model coordinates compiled functions, assembly wrappers, and startup code. PicoC adapts it to RETI; it does not implement the AMD64 ABI.
116-program-sections-interrupt-table-ent: Inline assembly calls the linked C helpers using the same RETI adaptation of the System V stack-frame rules.
23-saved-interrupt-stack-frame: Linux saves syscall context on the kernel stack. RETI entry and RTI use the active SP; PicoOS saves context on the user stack and has no memory isolation.
24-system-call-interface-and-execution: A library may expose familiar interfaces over different kernel syscalls. PicoOS also differs in signatures and behavior; familiar names do not imply binary compatibility.
241-syscall-selectors-and-register-conve: IN2 carries the syscall result just as it carries a PicoC function result. The wrapper and interrupt entry must agree on this register contract.
422-initial-argc-argv-and-envp: The Intel386 initial-stack model supplies the argc → argv → NULL → envp → NULL order. RETI adds an entry PC, uses word cells, fixes string order, and omits the auxiliary vector. POSIX defines the arrays and NAME=value strings, not their physical layout.
4221-concrete-initial-stack-example: argc counts the program name too; argv and envp are NULL-terminated pointer arrays. PicoOS prepares them during run rather than POSIX exec.
4321-parent-to-child-inheritance: PicoOS loads a fresh image instead of cloning the parent's memory. Loading and running copy different parts of the parent state.
4322-recording-termination-status: Reaping means final status collection and removal. PicoOS does not reparent orphaned children to init; it clears parent_pid and applies the configured parent-death signal.
731-supported-signals-and-fixed-actions: The null signal probes existence and permission without delivery. PicoOS checks only existence, has no user permissions or process-group PID forms, and rejects zombies.
734-fixed-picoos-signal-actions-compared: Unix/Linux allow catching or ignoring SIGINT, SIGTSTP, and SIGTTIN, but not SIGKILL or SIGSTOP. PicoOS gives all supported signals fixed actions.
81-per-process-file-descriptor-table: Unix descriptors can share an open-file description. PicoOS copies paths and scalar state into independent entries; copied file offsets subsequently diverge.
89-picoos-paths-working-directories-and-: The emulator independently confines paths to its root. POSIX traversal refuses symlinks; Linux also uses RESOLVE_BENEATH, RESOLVE_NO_SYMLINKS, and RESOLVE_NO_XDEV. Windows rejects reparse points.
1012-packing-arguments-and-executing-the: PicoOS waitpid takes one PID and returns the child status. POSIX waitpid has a status output parameter and options. The internal syscall request still passes a status pointer.
10291-streams-and-output-in-stdiopicoc: printf and fprintf find variadic arguments using the same stack-frame convention as ordinary PicoC calls.
1131-init-responsibilities: Init is the userspace supervisor: configure the environment, start a shell, wait for it, then start another session. Kernel initialization and dispatch remain kernel jobs.
126-inputoutput-redirection: Unix fork + exec / PicoOS load + run

A Unix shell redirects descriptors in a forked child before exec. PicoOS redirects its own table, runs the child with a copied snapshot, then restores itself. Lack of paging alone does not explain this choice.
1311-command-behavior-and-supported-opti: Names are familiar, but supported options differ. cd must be a shell built-in because it changes the shell's own working directory.
17-limitations: POSIX-like names support teaching comparisons; the implementation is an educational subset, not a conforming Unix environment.
